column48: 1. SSD-DC: HLA6 (Pit Interaction, strain, lower back)-Incident Description:  On 7/24/2025, at approximately 10:20 AM, the Associate (AA) was operating an Order Picker (OP) and exiting aisle 176/177 when they disconnected from wire guidance and turned left onto the main pit aisle. The AA drove onto the wrong side of the main pit aisle and was driving on the left hand side of the main pit aisle into oncoming traffic. The AA drove down to aisle 181/182 and made a 90 degree turn into the aisle 181/182. The distance to turn and enter into the aisle was short after the AA straightened out their OP. The AA stated they had reconnected to wire guidance upon entering aisle 182/183 but were not fully centered in the aisle as they approached the yellow end-cap guarding. The OP was off-centered to the left upon entry, causing the left outrigger to strike the yellow end-cap guarding. The impact sensor was triggered, stopping the OP outside of aisle 182/183. The abrupt stop caused the AA’s body to jolt forward, followed by a sudden halt, at which point the AA experienced pain in their lower back. A member of management (AM) was in the vicinity and responded to the incident. The AM helped secure the area and noticed that their harness was not adjusted appropriately. AM noticed that their harness was fitted tightly on their left side. AM coached AA on how to adjust their harness after AA stated they did not know how to adjust their harness. AM then escorted the AA to Amcare. The AA reported a pain level of 5 out of 10 at the time of the incident and was provided an instant ice pack for 15 minutes along with magnesium salicylate (580 mg) for pain relief. AA was provided a take home kit with ice packs and magnesium salicylate (580 mg) for pain relief. After treatment, the AA reported a pain level of 4 out of 10. The AA was not cleared to return to operating the OP and instead supported in an indirect role for the remainder of the shift. The AA is scheduled to retrain on the Order Picker during their next scheduled shift on 7/26/25

Incident Description_ BU – HLA6 (Near Miss, struck against) – On 9/21/25 AA was VNA picking, as the AA approached aisle 100-101 on the East side of the 100s traveling west bound. As the AA got closer to the entrance the AA turned on the wire guidance to allow the OP to connect and align and as the AA drove more into the entrance of the aisle that is when their Ops’ right side made impact with the yellow guard rail and immediately pushed to OP towards the middle of the aisle after it impacted and bounced off the guard rail. The AA was picking roughly 7.5 hours prior to the incident happening. 
Recordability Rationale_ -  N/A
Training – AA was trained for (DC 2-2-2: Case Pick) on 2025-08-25. 
Root Cause_ - After further investigation it was found that the root cause to the pit near miss was due to deviation from PMV on entering/exiting the aisle with wire guidance, the AA stated the beeping noise the OP makes when it is attempting to align was still beeping as they gassed it to enter the aisle prior to impact.  \a contributing factor to note was the blue corrugate shuttle outside the entrance of aisles 101/102 being close to the left side of aisle 101 which the AA noted also made her do a wider turn in a sense b/c of how close it was to the left side of the aisle. 
Corrective Action_ - 
a.   OP retrains for the AA and will have the learning team go over the wire guidance multiple times to make sure the AAs understand and know how to tell when the OP is aligned or not.  
b. Offer extra training/support for any LC1-LC3 pickers on OP usage, entering/exiting the aisles, and how to use the different mechanisms/tools on the Ops to their intended use to keep OP operators as safe as possible. 
c – Walk all aisles to see if any of the corrugate/Trash/Plastic bins are too close to their adjacent aisle to get them relocated or find better place to deploy them to ensure OP drivers have sufficient space for their OP maneuvers.

SSD-DC – HLA6 (Serious Incident Near Miss; Elevated PIT Stuck) – On 1/28/25 at 10:44 an associate escalated to leadership that they were stuck in the air on their OP in aisle 134/135 via Help Me app. The AA was in pick process path traveling eastbound on OP inside the aisle while at the same time descending from bin level N to bin level J to access their next pick (airplaning). During that movement, a bulky case that was sticking out of the bin got wedged between the right side of the OP and the bin, causing the OP to tilt to the left and get stuck. After consulting with safety, RME, and Raymond teams, operations contacted the fire department at 11:05. Visalia Fire Department arrived on scene at 11:09. The AA was safely brought down at 11:52 with no injuries. 

Root Cause: Upon further investigation it was discovered that the case (csXRJKz9nHd) was hanging out of bin P-1-V135J660. After reviewing the stow heat map, it was found VNA 134/135 was at 67% capacity at the time of the incident. Additionally, it was found that the case was stowed into the bin by a night shift associate on 1/15/25. The last touch of the bin was that same associate. Another contributing factor is the AA that got stuck in the aisle while descending down from level N while moving forward (airplaning) resulting in the case getting wedged between the bin and OP, stemming from a gap in OP training standards. The root cause is determined to be a lack of management of bin etiquette from stow, pick, and ICQA.

column48: On 8/19/2025 at approximately 1:56pm, A Goodyear tire vendor was performing maintenance in the trailer yard on the north east side of the building. While the vendor was inflating a trailer tire, the sidewall of the tire blew out, causing a loud boom that shook the building and was heard all the way on the south side of the building near dispatch. WHS, RME, and operations quickly entered the yard to investigate. Upon investigation it was found that the vendor was off to the side of the tire when it blew. On 12/31/2025 between approximately 5:45 a.m. and 6:20 a.m. Whole Foods vendor driver TCC74, delivering P.O. 2Q7YXABN to SAZ2, was managing their own TDR at dock door DD124 for an inbound appointment scheduled via Carrier Central. The shipment with Shipment ID 114897037989 was associated with Appointment ID 79310037989 and Appointment Reference Code SAZ4-WA-1108, with a scheduled arrival time of 06:30 MST and an actual arrival time of 06:03 MST. Actual processing began at 06:07 MST.

After unloading was completed and paperwork was returned, the vendor closed the dock door and exited the site without completing TDR OUT by disengaging the dock lock. The vendor managed TDR without final visual verification of dock lock disengagement. As a result, the dock lock remained engaged, which triggered the dock alarm when the vendor attempted to depart and prevented trailer movement.

The vendor returned inside the building and was escorted back to dock door DD124 to properly release the trailer. The dock alarm was deactivated while the trailer was still connected, and the vendor verbally confirmed that the dock lock had been released. The vendor was then escorted back to the cage area and exited the site without further issue.

No injuries, property damage, or trailer movement occurred. The event was classified as a near miss and logged as a vendor TDR OUT miss.

Incident Summary: On August 27, 2025, at approximately 4:22 PM, Operations dispatched RME via radio regarding a package jam on conveyor TL-09. MRT#1, responded to the call and proceeded to the equipment to assess the issue. Upon arrival, they observed the conveyor motor was running, and the belt was not moving. MRT#1 attempted to contact SMRT#1 over the radio for assistance; however, they did not respond. MRT#1 then pressed the emergency stop (E-stop) to halt the conveyor and began manually removing packages from the conveyor, placing them on the floor. After clearing several packages, they identified the cause of the jam — a package lodged in the flexco plates at the incline/hitch point of the conveyor. MRT#1 proceeded to the RME cage to retrieve a pry bar for jam removal. As they were returning to TL-09 with the pry bar, SMRT#1 was returning from lunch and observed MRT#1 walking toward the conveyor. SMRT#1 proceeded to the RME cage to get their personal locks in preparation to perform Lockout/Tagout (LOTO). At the same time, an Ops AM was also approaching the conveyor area. Upon arrival, SMRT#1 observed that the conveyor’s electrical disconnect had not been locked out and that MRT#1 was actively working inside the equipment, using the pry bar to remove the flexco plate. Recognizing the safety concern, SMRT#1 immediately exercised their Stop Work Authority and instructed MRT#1 to cease work and properly lock out the equipment. Despite this, MRT#1 continued the task, cleared the jammed package, and closed the side panel using the lock attached to the panel approximately one minute later. SMRT#1 reiterated to MRT#1 the importance of following LOTO procedures prior to performing work on equipment. MRT#1 acknowledged the concern but replied that they would follow the procedure but they did not.

At approximately 11:05 PM, a collision occurred between two Order Picker operators, AA 1 and AA 2, inside the VNA area. AA 1 exited his aisle and came to a full stop at the intersection as required. After honking and scanning, he began moving straight/right into the next aisle.

Due to the blind-spot created by the multi-aisle layout, AA 1 could not see traffic approaching from the left.

At the same time, AA 2 exited his aisle and began turning LEFT into the same intersection. Although his machine did come to a stop at the aisle exit, AA 2 did not properly scan, did not honk, and was not clipped into his required safety cage. AA 2 also admitted he “did not see” AA 1, showing lack of attention in the intersection.

As AA 2 proceeded with his left turn without confirming the area was clear, he drove directly into AA 1’s path. AA 2’s machine struck the front/side of AA 1’s order picker. No injuries were reported, but both machines sustained contact.

The primary contributing factors were AA 2’s inattention, failure to honk, failure to scan, and failure to wear the required safety cage, combined with the natural blind-spot created by the VNA layout.

'- Facts: The technician was informed of a smoke smell originating from the auger. Upon arrival, visible embers and smoke were observed. The technician contacted the manager, Rick Granberg, who advised them to shut down and detach the auger and to have the hostler pull the container away from the building. Once the container was removed and situated away from the building, emergency services (911) were called, and the building was evacuated as a precaution. DESCRIPTION- On 04/15/2026 at approximately 1357, A box of Cottonelle 30 Toilet paper rolls which is a very narrow aisle (VNA) item) was packed and placed onto the conveyor belt in an upright position. The package travelled along the conveyor which included an elevated portion of the conveyance. The package ascended with no issue but during the descend the package tumbled forward and fell towards the pack station table where it became jammed while still on the conveyor belt. During this time multiple VNA large items began to descend the conveyor resulting in an accumulation of packages. The conveyor did not stop as the accumulation began and the force of the VNA packages caused the pack table to tip forward and fall to the ground, striking a mobile cart. There were not associates near the area or working at the pack stations and no injuries.

ROOT CAUSE- EQUIPMENT/MACHINE- The building is one of the first generation of design standards, these generation buildings do not have the controls to prevent packages from moving off the conveyor on the descend. Newer version sites have a 2-inch side rail on the pack station side to prevent the packages from falling off the conveyor after the descend.

Incident Summary

An Amazon Associate operating a Order Picker was involved in a near-miss incident in the pick area. While navigating through a congested space with multiple Order Pickers (OPs), the Associate attempted to avoid contact with OPs to their front and side. During this maneuver, their OP's rear cage contacted a stationary OP's hood, causing the hood to detach. No injuries occurred. Operations immediately stopped work activities in the affected area, removed the Associate from equipment, conducted a standard AmCare assessment, and notified the Flow Area Manager. The incident investigation revealed two main contributing factors: area congestion due to multiple OPs and a Voluntary Time Off (VTO) announcement that caused rushed movement. A FANS message offering 15 VTO slots to pickers had resulted in Associates congregating at the pick desk, despite explicit instructions to remain on their OPs. According to the AA's statement, the contributing factors included area congestion and multiple obstacles requiring simultaneous attention. 
Root Cause:
The root cause of this near-miss incident was an inadequate Voluntary Time Off (VTO) management system that failed to account for its impact on floor safety and operations. The current VTO announcement process created an unintended "first-come, first-served" mentality, leading to a sudden rush of Associates abandoning their workstations and creating congestion in the pick area. This systemic flaw in the VTO process directly contributed to unsafe conditions, overriding existing safety protocols and training, and ultimately resulting in the near-miss incident with the Powered Industrial Truck (PIT).
Corrective Actions:
Implement mandatory spacing review training for all PIE operators (Owner: learning ECD: 11/6/2025)
Install visual markers/

SSD-FC: SIL1 - (Near miss - Transportation (Yard) (Contractor)) DESCRIPTION On 02/24/2026 at approximately 0321 PM, a 3P tractor driver from Easy Trucking LLC reversed into a slip to attach to an empty trailer. While attempting to leave with the trailer, the trailer detached from the 5th wheel causing the trailer to slide and tilt, nearly tipping over onto a flex vehicle parked outside of the overcrowded parking zone. The flex vehicle had an occupied driver inside the vehicle at the time of the incident. At the time of the incident, there were 8 vehicles parked outside of approved parking locations in the yard. Weather conditions at the time of the incident were overcast with a temperature of 34°F and no precipitation. There were no injuries sustained and no damage to Amazon property or equipment as a result of this incident. Following the incident, Leadership immediately secured the area and proceeded to conduct yard traffic control until Easy Trucking LLC dispatched tow truck service to lift the trailer and properly stabilize it to remove the trailer from the tractor. The onsite hostler moved the trailer back into its assigned slip after the scene was safely released. The site refused to allow the driver to take their scheduled trailer and instructed the driver to leave the site. Upon investigation, the 3P driver failed to perform the required tug test to validate the 5th wheel was properly coupled to the trailer. Additional investigation showed that the site's capacity planning exceeded the amount of physically available parking spots for Flex Drivers to safely park while on site. The incident occurred specifically in the trailer overflow lot of the SIL1 yard.
TRAINING: The 3P driver from Easy Trucking LLC was last issued a Class A CDL on 03/25/2024.

RC1 – The driver lacked the required knowledge, skills, and procedural awareness to safely couple a trailer and verify attachment per standard operating procedures.

On 04.23.26 at approximately 1455, a Prime Air associate was traversing the shared crosswalk connecting the SMI1 main entrance sidewalk to the Prime Air PADDC. The crosswalk is located on the shared roadway between the SMI1 flex yard and the Prime Air facility and is the required standard work path for Prime Air associates moving between the two buildings.

The Flex vehicle stopped in the crosswalk following the contact. The Prime Air associate then walked around the front of the stopped Flex vehicle and continued to the PADDC. No injuries were reported.

PA eventually maneuvered the empty pallet with the pallet jack to a nearby bollard. PA braced empty pallet behind the bollard and was able to pull the pallet jack free. OM counseled PA that if pallet jack is stuck, do not have anybody place a foot/body weight on top of empty pallet.

Detailed definition of the incident:
On July 10, 2025, at approximately 02:22 a.m., a near-miss incident was identified involving an Associate assigned to a VNA Stow aisle 107–108 location. The Manager, while conducting routine checks, discovered the AA asleep while elevated in the VNA aisle during their scheduled assignment. The AA was unresponsive at first but awoke shortly after being addressed by the Manager. No injury or damage to equipment occurred as a result of the incident.

The AM immediately escalated the situation to the Ops Manager, who arrived at the scene to assess the condition of the AA. The OM escorted the AA to the on-site wellness center (AMCARE) for evaluation. The AA was able to walk unassisted and was uninjured. After a preliminary assessment at AMCARE, no medical treatment was required; however, the AA was advised to rest and monitor their condition. The AA was removed from OP operations and later decided to go home due to exhaustion and a desire to rest for the night.

After the investigation, it was identified that the Associate had been in the same process path for the past four days, performing the same task in VNA. Due to the elevated volume during Prime Week and the repetitive nature of the task, the AA reported that stowing heavy items throughout the shift contributed to their exhaustion, which may have caused them to fall asleep on the OP while elevated. The AA was trained on the process path on January 21, 2025, and the last PIT SGT was conducted on June 11, 2025.

Video footage was requested from the on-site security team and will be sent to on-site HR for future investigation. The AA’s badge has been suspended for operating the order picker and they will be placed in retraining after the investigation is completed.

AA’s Statement:

"I had to sit down to stow cat litter since it was heavy and I must have fallen asleep. The next thing I remember is my manager calling me and asking if I was okay. I am not hurt or injured—nothing serious happened—I’m just exhausted for the night."

Date/Time: October 8, 2025, at approximately 10:30 a.m.
Location: Dock Door 106
Incident Type: Near-Miss (TDR Protocol)

Description of Incident:
At approximately 10:30 a.m., a near-miss incident occurred at Dock Door 106 involving Area Manager Manish K. The issue was identified by Manager Emily G during routine tasks.

It was observed that the dock lock and dock plate were engaged with the trailer; however, the TDR In indicator was not flipped to reflect completion. This created a condition where the trailer appeared to be TDR’d in, but the process had not been properly completed—resulting in a near miss.

No injuries or equipment damage occurred.

Immediate Actions Taken:

The incident was escalated to Operations Manager Mo A.

Caleb H conducted a “seek-to-understand” discussion with Manish K regarding the incident.

Manager Statement (Manish K):
Manish reported that he had instructed a driver to back the trailer into Dock Door 106 to verify alignment. He engaged the dock lock, opened the roll-up door, and engaged the dock plate. However, he did not flip the TDR indicator because he was not conducting a full TDR—only checking alignment.

During the process, he was called over the radio by Managers Alex and Emily for another task. In a hurry, he left the dock in its current state without completing the proper TDR procedure or resetting the equipment.

Investigation Findings:

Manager Manish K failed to properly complete the TDR process after engaging the dock equipment.

He did not follow TDR protocol, specifically failing to respond appropriately to radio calls while in the middle of the TDR task.

His actions resulted in an incomplete TDR and a near-miss safety incident.

Conclusion:
The incident was a result of procedural non-compliance and lack of task focus while performing TDR responsibilities.

column48: SSD SOR3 – GTDR Indicator Miss - Description – on 1/13/2025 During an audit of GTDR logs it was discovered that a TDR docking was completed without the indicator being set to complete. The AA had worked in this process path for 0.5 on the day of incident. 12:12:28: A paper towel holder (ASIN: unknown) wedged into the conveyance at the waterfall drop on the 1100/1200 side corner.

12:22:59: Multiple packages dislodged from jam, went down the waterfall, and jammed packages bunched higher up the conveyance.

12:54:54: Jammed packages were back ~30 feet from the wedged package.

SSD: HPA1 - (Falling/Flying Objects; Near Miss) - Description – On 03/11/2026 at approximately 10:07 AM, an Associate (AA) working in Transfer Support, Transfer Dock Crew, experienced a near miss while down-stacking two pallets on a dock plate with stand up RC-40. The associate was working at DD142 and had stacked both pallets on the dock plate and was preparing to down-stack them. The AA noticed a problem with one of the pallets and got off the Stand Up to inspect both pallets. They then returned to the Stand Up, placed the forks back under the bottom pallet, and began pushing the pallets back into the truck. When asked why they decided to push the pallets back rather than pull off the top pallet first, the associate stated they were trying to fix the pallets. As soon as they started pushing, the bottom pallet's side began to bow out. The AA immediately pulled the forks out from under the pallet, and the pallet then fully collapsed. Management reviewed the contents of both pallets and found that the bottom pallet was not stacked to the top and contained lighter packages, while the top pallet contained more packages that were heavier than those on the bottom pallet.
Training – The AA was trained in all processes related to trailer unload. Training was completed on 09/25/2025, and the AA has been in the PATH program for a total of 5.5 months. The AA stated, "The bottom pallet was too light and the top pallet was too heavy, so when I pulled it, the two pallets fell."
Root Cause – The UPP spilled over due to improper stacking when loaded into the trailer. The top UPP was significantly heavier than the bottom UPP, which was only halfway full. column48: SSD-FC: STN1 - (Near miss - Transportation (TDR and Load Quality) (Amazon Associate)) DESCRIPTION- On 02/12/2026 at approximately 0532 AM, an An Amazon Associate executed a TDR in transaction for DD 216, then subsequently cancelled the transaction through the Dolphin. The AA was working in PA/TDR process path at the time. During operations, the associate stated they began feeling ill approximately one hour after completing the initial TDR process. While moving to the back room due to illness, the associate stated the dolphin handheld device hit the ground, causing screen malfunction and random automatic selections that resulted in the unintended TDR cancellation in the virtual system.  ROOT CAUSE- Associate health emergency during critical TDR operations combined with equipment vulnerability to physical damage. The dropped dolphin device malfunctioned and began making erratic system inputs automatically, leading to uncontrolled transaction processing. Contributing factors include lack of emergency protocols for securing handheld devices during health incidents and system susceptibility to inputs from damaged hardware. During my investigation It shows that a TDR can be cancelled after a TDR in was completed. A TDR can be canceled with two touches to the dolphin, one on the exit and one on yes to authorize cancel. SSD DC: HTX3 – (Near Miss – Struck Against) – Description
On 12/10/2025 at approximately 1:40 PM, an AA working in Pick had a near miss in aisle 224 at the beginning of the aisle. The AA was attempting to come into aisle 224. AA stated they started connecting their OP to the wire guidance before the yellow line, and the OP stopped beeping, resulting in the OP not connecting to the wire guide properly.
This prompted the associate to back up, turn off the wire guide connection, and attempt to turn it back on for a second alignment. However, upon proceeding forward, the AA believed the wire guidance was reactivated but failed to align the OP correctly to the wire guidance.
A further investigation found that the AA had overshot the intended aisle by approximately 3 feet, causing them to make a quick U-turn to realign into aisle 224. During this maneuver, the OP approached the aisle misaligned, which became a contributing factor.
As a result, the OP lightly struck the yellow end cap at the beginning of the aisle. Leadership arrived shortly after and instructed the AA to step away from operating the OP until assistance arrived.
There were no injuries, no paint transfer, no damages, and no product involvement.
The AA is a Night Shift associate who accepted VET for Day Shift and had been working in this process path for 6 hours prior to the near miss.

The AA was hired on 11/17/2025 and received PIT training on 11/18/2025.

SSD: HTX3 - (OP Incident) - An Associate (AA) reported that their Powered Industrial Truck (PIT) displayed error code. OPS contacted Reliability Maintenance Engineering (RME) for assistance on behalf the AA. RME performed a code reset and cleared the error code, telling the associate the equipment was safe to use. While stowing, the associate became stuck and requested help through the Help Me app at 22:49. The Operations team responded to the scene and, upon realizing the associate was stuck, contacted RME and Safety for support. When they were unable to resolve the situation, OPS called Emergency Medical Services (EMS) at 23:43. EMS arrived at 00:09 and successfully evacuated the associate using a scissors lift, departing at 00:25. During the subsequent Seek to understand with Operations, Learning team, and Malin (maintenance vendor), two key findings emerged: first, RME personnel are not authorized to clear error codes yet and should have instructed the associate to red tag the equipment; second, the incident occurred because the associate's PIT forks were positioned on the racks, causing the equipment to become stuck because of the tension.

Incident Description: On 01/14/2026, an associate was operating a tugger in the car wash area near staging zone 25. The associate was parked in a non-loading zone that was difficult to exit from, positioned away from the car wash exit with an A-safe barrier to their left side and empty cages crossing the staging zone barrier. When attempting to reverse toward the right side, where another tugger was positioned behind loaded cages, the associate stated, "I was checking my right side for cages, but by mistake didn't check my left side because I was so focused on checking my right side and hit the corner railing." There were cages on the right side of where the tugger was parked, as well as another tugger that was dropping off cages and did not maintain the required 8-foot distance.

CCTV footage confirmed the associate was parked in a non-loading zone in a congested area with another tugger associate who was not within the required 8-foot distance. Prior to attempting to back up their tugger, the associate was checking their right side for the other tugger associate and cages but did not check their left side where the A-safe barrier was located. An empty cage positioned next to the associate may have also focused more of their attention to the right-hand side. The associate was on their fourth day of the work week.

Training: The associate completed tugger training on 12/02/2025 and had been operating the equipment for over a month at the time of the incident.

Root Cause: The associate parked in a non-loading zone and was positioned too close to other cages and associates, creating a congested work environment that limited visibility and safe maneuvering space.

Corrective Actions:

The incident was not promptly reported to the area supervisor, who initiated standard safety protocols.

Also, CCTV footage (1107) shows AA turning into aisle 184-185 at a shallow angle. No injuries were reported as a result of this incident, and there was no operational downtime. SSD-FC: HTX3 - (Near Miss - Order Picker (Amazon Associate)) On 04/30/2026 at approximately 04:40 AM, an AA operating Order Picker (OP) 089 in Transfer-Out Pick process path, was involved in a near miss going into aisle 103 in the VNA area. The AA had exited Aisle 105 and was transitioning into Aisle 103. While the OP was still in motion, the AA attempted to flip the switch to activate the guidance system. As the switch was engaged, the OP shifted left and struck the corner of the VNA rack at Aisle 103. No injuries were sustained. Facility equipment involved includes OP 089 and the VNA rack structure at Aisle 103.

TRAINING — The AA was trained on this function on 04/22/2026 (module: DC_ORDER_PICKER. The AA had 8 days of tenure at the time of the near miss.

AA STATEMENT — The AA stated they were turning into Aisle 103 after exiting Aisle 105 and attempted to activate the guidance system switch while the OP was still moving. As the switch was flipped, the OP moved left and made contact with the corner of the VNA rack. 

ROOT CAUSE — Distracted AA while operating OP. The AA attempted to activate the VNA guidance system switch while the OP was still in motion during the transition from Aisle 105 to Aisle 103. The act of flipping the switch while moving divided the AA's attention and altered the OP's trajectory, resulting in contact with the VNA rack.

ACTION- Coach AAs the safe distance from when they exit the aisles to when they're able to turn and go into the aisle next to it.

column48: SSD: HTX3 (Lower abdomen, left leg and left foot exposure to or contact with) On 11/9/25 at approximately 1:39am in line load, an incident occurred involving a chemical spill of “Ortho Home Defense Insect Killer for Indoor and Perimeter2 with Comfort Wand, Controls Ants, Roaches, Spiders and More, 1.33 gal.” The associate was lifting a box that was tilted on its side from a cage to place it onto the conveyor. The associate did not notice the box was wet before lifting it. Later, they observed that the bottom of the box was wet and removed it from the conveyor before it reached the sorter. During the lift, they felt liquid spill onto their waist and leg, dripping down to their feet.  The associate immediately escalated the incident to a PA who instructed them to wipe off the exposed areas. The associate went to the bathroom and used water and paper towels to clean the affected areas while leadership investigated the cause of the leakage. It was discovered that the box contained multiple cases of Ortho Home Defense insect killer, with only one case leaking. Once the PA identified the chemical, the associate was instructed to visit wellness for treatment. Leadership placed the damaged item in the designated damages area. During the investigation, the recommended first aid for skin contact with the chemical was to flush the contaminated area with plenty of water and remove contaminated clothing and shoes. The associate reported no pain or irritation, was wearing the required PPE, and had completed safety school training on September 20, 2025. Upon further investigation, it was determined that the associate was not trained in line load operations, only in turret for pallet stow and tugger. Additionally, the Physician and Nurse on Demand were not called. The associate was VTO’d and sent home after the incident. Root Cause - Failure to complete a 6-sided check before lifting the case in line load. Additionally, contributing factors include the failure to escalate damaged cases during picking. On October 3, 2025, at 8:55 PM, an Associate (AA) was involved in a minor equipment incident at aisle 180-181. The Associate, who had less than one month of experience in this process path, contacted a yellow safety corner guard while operating a cage vehicle during their regular shift. As the AA approached the aisle entrance, they turned on the guidance wire to enter the aisle as entering the aisle the OP was adjusting itself aligning to the wire and bumped into the yellow corner safety guard. The incident occurred under standard lighting conditions, with all safety markings and barriers properly installed and visible. No environmental factors contributed to the occurrence. Immediately following the contact, the area was inspected for damage, and the equipment was examined for operational safety. The incident was not reported to the area supervisor. PA reported incident as soon as it was seen. AM then initiated standard safety protocols.
Upon investigation, it was determined that the Associate was told by a learning ambassador when turning on the guidance wire to not even touch the steering and trust the machine when going into the aisle. Also, they were trained not to touch wheel when wire guide was on. No injuries were reported as a result of this incident, and there was no operational downtime. Both the equipment and the barrier remained in serviceable condition, with the barrier sustaining minimal contact and no structural compromise.
As a preventive measure, the Associate has been scheduled for refresher training on usage of wire guidance and when to turn the wire guidance on and off. Additionally, management will conduct teaching to all Learning Ambassadors on the instruction- of how to properly use the wire guidance. This incident highlights the importance of thorough training for new Associates and continuous evaluation of workplace safety measures

On September 17, 2025, between 0500 and 1000, a SEV event on the TR1-10 conveyance line at SVA2 to repair an Intralox conveyor belt. The Sev required response from multiple technicians across overlapping shifts. The incident focused on repeated breaches of the WHS Hazardous Energy Control Procedure, specifically related to the Lockout/Tagout (LOTO) process. Two technicians performed equipment work without proper LOTO application to the electrical and pneumatic lockout points, even after receiving a verbal safety reminder. Additionally, there were instances of PPE non-compliance, with multiple technicians observed without required bump caps and gloves in the work area. The situation was further complicated by a mismatch between the submitted Pre-Task Plan (PTP) and the actual work performed.

SAFETY VIOLATIONS
•	WHS Hazardous Energy Control Procedure Violations
•	Failure to properly implement LOTO process
•	Misrepresentation of work scope on PTP (belt tracking vs. belt repair)
•	Unauthorized equipment access after safety intervention
•	No boundary enclosing the entire work area using Red “Danger” tape at a minimum distance of 5 feet (1.5M) or at the determined.
•	PPE Non-Compliance
•	Multiple technicians without required bump caps and gloves in work area

AM1 who removed the dock guardian stated, they did not know the PIT was in the trailer and closed the guardian when they saw the PIT exit the trailer

PIT operator stated, they spoke to AM2 and was told AM2 would be unloading the injection trailer and they stepped off the PIT and began pulling work out with a pallet jack. PIT operator stated when they got back on the PIT they didn’t see AM2
Training – The PIT AA was last trained 5/4/2024

column48: (Near Miss - Struck Tugger Against) On 11/8/25 at approximately 9:37pm, A PA was operating a tugger pulling 5 empty carts through Zone 24 when an incident occurred. While attempting to navigate an "S" turn around the maps cage area, the third cart collided with the bottom pole of an A-Safe barrier. The PA immediately stopped the tugger, dismounted to inspect for potential damages, and subsequently reported the incident to the AM and Safety team. During the investigation, it was discovered that the tugger, designated for pick operations, had originally been verbally assigned to pallet stow by the Stow AM, leaving the pick team without their needed indirect role. This indirect shortage, combined with lack of pick HC and poor at shift handoff (with only 4 empty cages available), forced the PA to operate the tugger due to the lack of available tugger operators. Additionally, the PA raised concerns about the width of certain tugger lanes, noting they were too narrow and required expansion to ensure safe operations. PA completed tugger training on 9/5/2025 and was wearing all required PPE. Physcian and Nurse on demand was not called, with 0 pain to report. Root cause - While operating the tugger, the driver failed to maintain adequate clearance between the equipment and the A-Safe barrier when executing the turn. Contributing to this incident was the insufficient width between A-Safe barriers, which created a challenging environment for safe tugger operation. Corrective Actions – (1) Senior Change Management Ops and WHS Manager will conduct a thorough assessment to evaluate the width of tugger turn corners, with the goal of identifying areas that require expansion to allow for safer turning radius. (2) The PA involved in the incident will undergo comprehensive tugger retraining to reinforce proper operating procedures and turning techniques. (3) BHN Pick team will identify 2 associates to train for tugger to increase indirect role HC to fill shift gaps.

Contributing factors noted of insufficient tools to monitor last touch of bins to allow for last touch feedbacks to be input. Lack of sufficient tools allowed for drift in the picking process due to inadequate enforcement of procedures.

This should include daily checks for protruding pallets or other potential obstructions, with a system for immediate correction of any identified issues. AA was picking in aisle 188 at the time of the incident and according to their statement they were navigating from a pick at M level (P-1-V188M370) and lowered themselves to get to the next bin. It was also determined through diving deep that the K-level bin above was the origination for the bin divider.
